results.name: digit_rule_below_min_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of 3+ examples all sharing one final digit, yes rate for targets with that same final digit lying below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend a final-digit rule downward past the examples more than the model (with its span-restricted runs) predicts, below null means they confine the rule to the examples' stretch more strongly.
results.code:
# name: digit_rule_below_min_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 3+ examples all sharing one final digit, yes rate for targets with that same final digit lying below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend a final-digit rule downward past the examples more than the model (with its span-restricted runs) predicts, below null means they confine the rule to the examples' stretch more strongly.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    n = parts.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    vals = parts.values
    d = np.mod(vals, 10)
    d0 = d[:, 0]
    same = np.all((d == d0[:, None]) | np.isnan(vals), axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(vals, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    m = (n >= 3) & same & (np.mod(t, 10) == d0) & (t < mn)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: lag1_same_set_carryover
results.description: Within a participant, among consecutive trials sharing the same set, P(yes | previous yes) minus P(yes | previous no); observed above null means responses perseverate (or set-level belief drifts) beyond what the stimulus-driven model produces, below null means alternation.
results.code:
# name: lag1_same_set_carryover
# description: Within a participant, among consecutive trials sharing the same set, P(yes | previous yes) minus P(yes | previous no); observed above null means responses perseverate (or set-level belief drifts) beyond what the stimulus-driven model produces, below null means alternation.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].values == 0).cumsum()
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    s = df["number_set"].values
    ok = (pid[1:] == pid[:-1]) & (s[1:] == s[:-1])
    prev = r[:-1][ok]
    cur = r[1:][ok]
    a = cur[prev == 1]
    b = cur[prev == 0]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate for non-example targets within 6 of the last-shown example minus yes rate for those within 6 of the first-shown example (targets near both excluded); nonzero observed vs null means example order matters (recency > 0 / primacy < 0), which the order-blind model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate for non-example targets within 6 of the last-shown example minus yes rate for those within 6 of the first-shown example (targets near both excluded); nonzero observed vs null means example order matters (recency > 0 / primacy < 0), which the order-blind model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    n = parts.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    first = parts[0].values
    vals = parts.values
    last = vals[np.arange(len(vals)), n - 1]
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    isex = (vals == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    dl = np.abs(t - last)
    dfst = np.abs(t - first)
    base = (n >= 2) & (~isex)
    near_l = base & (dl <= 6) & (dfst > 6)
    near_f = base & (dfst <= 6) & (dl > 6)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    if near_l.sum() == 0 or near_f.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near_l].mean() - r[near_f].mean())

results.name: participant_yes_rate_spread
results.description: SD across participants (rows blocked by session, a new participant starting at each trial_index 0) of the overall yes rate; observed above null means people differ in yes-bias more than the model's single shared decision criterion produces.
results.code:
# name: participant_yes_rate_spread
# description: SD across participants (rows blocked by session, a new participant starting at each trial_index 0) of the overall yes rate; observed above null means people differ in yes-bias more than the model's single shared decision criterion produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].values == 0).cumsum()
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    tot = np.bincount(pid, weights=r)
    cnt = np.bincount(pid)
    m = cnt > 0
    return float(np.std(tot[m] / cnt[m]))

results.name: parity_violation_in_range
results.description: Among sets of 3+ examples that all share parity, yes rate for opposite-parity targets strictly inside the example range; observed above null means people fill in the range ignoring parity more than the model predicts (below null: they respect the parity rule more strongly than the model).
results.code:
# name: parity_violation_in_range
# description: Among sets of 3+ examples that all share parity, yes rate for opposite-parity targets strictly inside the example range; observed above null means people fill in the range ignoring parity more than the model predicts (below null: they respect the parity rule more strongly than the model).
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    n = parts.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    vals = parts.values
    p = np.mod(vals, 2)
    p0 = p[:, 0]
    same = np.all((p == p0[:, None]) | np.isnan(vals), axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(vals, axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(vals, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    m = (n >= 3) & same & (np.mod(t, 2) != p0) & (t > mn) & (t < mx)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: far_below_min_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets below half the smallest example, among sets whose smallest example is at least 20; observed below null means people treat the smallest example as a floor (penalising downward extrapolation) which the model, with only an upward ceiling, under-penalises; above null the reverse.

results.name: round_number_target_bonus
results.description: For sets containing no multiple of 10, yes rate on non-example multiple-of-10 targets minus yes rate on targets 1-3 away from a multiple of 10, both within 15 of some example; observed above null means people favour round-number targets beyond what the model's concepts predict (below null: they disfavour them).
results.code:
# name: round_number_target_bonus
# description: For sets containing no multiple of 10, yes rate on non-example multiple-of-10 targets minus yes rate on targets 1-3 away from a multiple of 10, both within 15 of some example; observed above null means people favour round-number targets beyond what the model's concepts predict (below null: they disfavour them).
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    vals = parts.values
    has10 = np.any(np.mod(vals, 10) == 0, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(vals - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    k = np.mod(t, 10)
    dist10 = np.minimum(k, 10 - k)
    base = (~has10) & (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 15)
    a = base & (dist10 == 0)
    b = base & (dist10 >= 1) & (dist10 <= 3)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: small_vs_large_max_overshoot_gap
results.description: Yes rate for targets 1-12 above the largest example when that maximum is at most 40, minus the same when the maximum is 55-88; observed below null means a fixed absolute overshoot is penalised even more above small maxima than the model's log-ratio criterion implies, above null means the ratio scaling overstates the small-vs-large asymmetry.
results.code:
# name: small_vs_large_max_overshoot_gap
# description: Yes rate for targets 1-12 above the largest example when that maximum is at most 40, minus the same when the maximum is 55-88; observed below null means a fixed absolute overshoot is penalised even more above small maxima than the model's log-ratio criterion implies, above null means the ratio scaling overstates the small-vs-large asymmetry.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    mx = parts.max(axis=1).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    ov = t - mx
    near = (ov >= 1) & (ov <= 12)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = near & (mx <= 40)
    b = near & (mx >= 55) & (mx <= 88)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
